```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE)
```

> **The brief.** A friend wants to invest in a flat in València and rent it on Airbnb. She has questions: *Where? What kind of listing? At what price?* You are her data scientist. Today we turn the raw data into a clean, analysis-ready table; in Session 2 we interrogate it and answer her.
>
> **The data.** [Inside Airbnb](https://insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/) publishes quarterly snapshots of every Airbnb listing in ~100 cities, València included. We work with the **frozen snapshot from Poliformat** (`data/` folder inside your RStudio project) so that everyone has identical data.

**Today's route** — every stop uses the project data:

| Block | ⏱ | What we learn |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · First contact | 45′ | the pipe, `read_csv`, `glimpse`, `skim`, `count`, `distinct` |
| 2 · Cleaning | 75′ | `stringr`, `parse_number`, `lubridate`, NA strategy |
| 3 · Transform, tidy & join | 60′ | dplyr verbs, grouped summaries, pivots, joins |
| 4 · Wrap-up | — | save with `write_rds`, today in one slide |

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)   # readr, dplyr, tidyr, stringr, lubridate, forcats, ggplot2...
library(janitor)     # clean_names() and friends
library(skimr)       # data overview
```

```{r snapshot-date}
# The date the snapshot was taken - our "today" for every date computation.
# (Why not Sys.Date()? Because the analysis must give the same answer next year.)
snapshot_date <- ymd("2026-07-02")
```

# Block 1 · First contact with the data ⏱ 45′

One tool before the data: the **pipe** `|>`. It feeds the result on its left into the function on its right, so code reads like a recipe — *take the data, and then filter, and then summarise*:

```{r}
# these two lines are identical:
sum(c(3, 7, 1, 9, 4) %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4))
c(3, 7, 1, 9, 4) %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4) |> sum()
```

From here on, everything is pipes.

`readr::read_csv()` reads CSV files — including gzip-compressed ones, no unzipping needed — into a **tibble** (a modern data frame: same thing, better printing, fewer surprises):

```{r read-listings}
listings_raw <- read_csv("data/listings.csv.gz")
dim(listings_raw)
```

> 💡 **About that parsing message.** When `read_csv()` prints its column specification, read it — it says what type it guessed for every column:
>
> * it usually guesses well, dates included;
> * the catch: it only looks at the first 1000 rows (`guess_max`). A column whose first 1000 values are blank gets guessed as `logical` and mis-parses from row 1001 on — the #1 "my import is broken" bug with real Inside Airbnb files;
> * if readr reports parsing problems, `problems()` lists them.

First look — three habits, in order:

* `glimpse()` — the table turned sideways: every column, its type, first values. Your map of what exists.
* `select() |> head()` — zoom into the few columns you care about right now.
* `skim()` — the full medical check-up: types, missing values, distributions.

```{r}
glimpse(listings_raw)      # every column, its type, first values
```

```{r}
listings_raw |> select(id, name, neighbourhood_cleansed, room_type, price,
                       host_since, last_review) |> head()
```

```{r skim, results='hide'}
skim(listings_raw)         # full quality report: types, NAs, distributions
# (output hidden in the knitted version - run it live, it is long and worth it)
```

Two workhorse questions you will ask of every dataset from now on:

* `n_distinct(x)` — how many *different* values does `x` take? (HW0's `length(unique(x))`, in one word)
* `count(col)` — a frequency table: one row per distinct value, its count in a column named `n`; `sort = TRUE` puts the biggest first:

```{r}
n_distinct(listings_raw$host_id)                 # how many different hosts?
listings_raw |> count(room_type, sort = TRUE)    # how many of each type?
```

Column names here are already clean `snake_case`. Real-world files often aren't (`"Fecha Alta"`, `"% Ocupación"`...) — make `janitor::clean_names()` a reflex first step:

```{r}
listings_raw <- listings_raw |> clean_names()    # a no-op here, a lifesaver elsewhere
```

Every column's meaning is documented in the official [data dictionary](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iWCNJcSutYqpULSQHlNyGInUvHg2BoUGoNRIGa6Szc4/edit) — keep it open, always.

🧰 **Sprint toolbox** — every function you need, in one glance. All the verbs are used piped, e.g. `listings_raw |> count(room_type)`. (`filter`, `mutate` and `summarise` get their proper treatment in Block 3; for now, use them exactly as sketched here.)

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `dim(df)` · `nrow(df)` | table dimensions · number of rows |
| `n_distinct(x)` | how many *different* values `x` contains |
| `count(col, sort = TRUE)` | frequency table of `col`, biggest first (can take several columns) |
| `filter(condition)` | keep only the rows where the condition is TRUE |
| `mutate(new = expr)` | add a new column computed from existing ones |
| `summarise(name = fun(col))` | collapse the table to one summary row (`min()`, `mean()`, ...) |
| `mean(is.na(x))` | share of missing values — the TRUE-counts-as-1 trick from HW0 |

1. How many listings and how many variables do we have?
2. How many different hosts? So, on average, how many listings per host?
3. What share of listings is each `room_type`? (`count()` + `mutate()`)
4. The 5 neighbourhoods (`neighbourhood_cleansed`) with most listings
5. How many listings have **never** been reviewed? (`number_of_reviews`)
6. What share of listings has no `price`? Can we answer "what does an Airbnb cost" ignoring this?

# Block 2 · Cleaning: types, text, dates, NAs ⏱ 75′

Look closely at what `read_csv()` could *not* solve for us:

```{r}
listings_raw |> select(price, bathrooms_text, host_is_superhost,
                       license, amenities) |> head()
```

`price` is text. `bathrooms_text` is text. `license` is a long tangle of text. This is normal: **real data arrives as strings**, and turning strings into usable variables is where a data scientist earns their salary.

## 2.1 · Money: `price` → number

`price` looks like `"$1,050.00"` (the file uses a `$` prefix whatever the real currency — here it means euros). `readr::parse_number()` extracts the number and ignores the decoration:

```{r}
listings <- listings_raw |>
  mutate(price_eur = parse_number(price))

listings |> select(price, price_eur) |> filter(!is.na(price)) |> head(4)
listings |> summarise(n_missing = sum(is.na(price_eur)),
                      share_missing = mean(is.na(price_eur)))
```

About 7% of prices are missing — modest, but **never silently drop rows** before asking why they're missing. Our policy, stated out loud: keep all rows; for *price* analyses use the subset with known price. And before shrugging "it's just 7%", check whether the missingness is random or *structural*:

```{r}
# is missing price random - or structural? Compare against availability:
listings |>
  group_by(no_availability = availability_365 == 0) |>
  summarise(share_na_price = mean(is.na(price_eur)), n = n())
```

Not random at all: listings with **zero availability** in the coming year are missing their price ~99% of the time — the price is missing *because* the listing is not currently on the market. (In some snapshots this pushes overall missingness above 30%.)

> 💡 **So can we drop them?** It depends on the question being asked:
>
> * *"What does booking a night cost?"* — dropping is fine. The price-less listings aren't bookable, so they aren't part of that market.
> * *"What could my flat charge?"* — dropping is biased. The missing prices belong to inactive listings, not to a random sample.
> * The rule: dropping NAs is only safe when the missingness has nothing to do with the question.

## 2.2 · Logicals in disguise: `"t"` / `"f"`

In the raw file, `host_is_superhost` and `instant_bookable` are coded `"t"`/`"f"` — and if you check `glimpse()`, they are *already* `<lgl>`: readr recognized the coding and parsed them for us. Verify, and note the NAs:

```{r}
listings |> count(host_is_superhost)
```

Don't rely on that luck. Files coded `"yes"/"no"`, `"Sí"/"No"` or `"0"/"1"`-as-text arrive as character, and then the conversion idiom is yours to apply:

```{r}
# the general pattern (a no-op here, since readr already did it):
# listings |> mutate(host_is_superhost = host_is_superhost == "yes")
```

> ⚠️ And never "convert" a column without checking its current type first — running `x == "t"` on an already-logical column silently turns every value into `FALSE`. Check with `class()` or `glimpse()`, *then* transform.

## 2.3 · Text surgery with stringr: `bathrooms_text`

`"1 bath"`, `"1.5 baths"`, `"2 shared baths"`, `"Half-bath"` — three pieces of information tangled in one string: how many, shared or private, and a special word for ½.

```{r}
listings |> count(bathrooms_text, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)

listings <- listings |>
  mutate(
    # first rewrite the special case as text, then parse - no warnings, no branches:
    baths        = parse_number(
                     str_replace(bathrooms_text,
                                 regex("half-?bath", ignore_case = TRUE), "0.5")),
    baths_shared = str_detect(bathrooms_text, "shared")
  )

listings |> count(baths, baths_shared, sort = TRUE) |> head(6)
```

In words:

* `baths` — first rewrite the awkward case (`"Half-bath"` → `"0.5"`, any capitalisation), *then* let `parse_number()` read the leading number of every string;
* `baths_shared` — ask each string whether the word `"shared"` appears;
* net result: one tangled column became two clean ones — a number and a logical.

The `stringr` trio to remember:

* `str_detect()` — is the pattern there?
* `str_remove()` / `str_replace()` — delete it / swap it;
* `str_extract()` — pull the matching piece out.

All three take regular expressions — of which we use only a pinch in this course.

## 2.4 · Time with lubridate

`read_csv` already parsed `first_review` and `last_review` as dates (ISO format helps). When it doesn't — or when you need to compute with dates — **lubridate** is the toolbox. The essentials in one glance:

* **parse text → date** — `ymd("2026-07-02")`, `dmy("02/07/2026")`, `mdy(...)`: pick the function spelling the order the text is written in (`ymd_hms()` and friends for date-times);
* **build from pieces** — `make_date(year, month, day)`;
* **extract components** — `year()`, `month()`, `day()`, `wday(label = TRUE)` for the weekday, `hour()`;
* **round** — `floor_date(date, "month")`: every date down to the 1st of its month;
* **arithmetic** — `interval(start, end)` measured with `time_length(span, "years")`; add or subtract calendar periods with `months(12)`, `days(7)`; `today()` is today.

In our data:

```{r}
listings <- listings |>
  mutate(
    listing_age_yrs   = time_length(interval(first_review, snapshot_date), "years"),
    months_since_rev  = time_length(interval(last_review, snapshot_date), "months"),
    is_active         = !is.na(last_review) & last_review >= snapshot_date - months(12)
  )

listings |> summarise(mean_age = mean(listing_age_yrs, na.rm = TRUE),
                      share_active = mean(is_active))
```

Line by line:

* `interval(first_review, snapshot_date)` — the time span between two dates;
* `time_length(span, "years")` — measure that span in the unit you choose (fractional years here);
* `is_active` reads as a sentence: *has a last review, and it falls within the 12 months before the snapshot* — `months(12)` is lubridate's "twelve calendar months", varying month lengths handled for you.


> ⚠️ You'd naturally compute *host tenure* from `host_since` — but in this snapshot `host_since` (and `host_response_*`) arrive **completely empty**. Real sources drift: columns appear, empty out, change format. Check before you trust — and keep a plan B (here: `first_review` as the listing's age on the market).

## 2.5 · Sneaky non-NAs: `na_if()`

**Missingness wears costumes**: `"N/A"`, `"unknown"`, `999`, `"-"` — values that *mean* missing but that R happily treats as valid data. `na_if(x, value)` turns one disguise into a real NA:

```{r}
rates <- c("92%", "88%", "N/A", "100%")
parse_number(na_if(rates, "N/A"))
```

Audit every categorical column with `count()` before trusting it — in several Inside Airbnb snapshots `host_response_time` carries literal `"N/A"` strings (in ours it arrives empty instead). Alternative at import time: `read_csv(..., na = c("", "N/A"))`.

🧰 **Sprint toolbox** — the new pieces for this sprint (everything else you've just seen in action):

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `case_when(cond ~ value, ..., TRUE ~ default)` | multi-branch if/else inside `mutate()`: conditions are tried top to bottom, first match wins, `TRUE ~ ...` is the catch-all. E.g. `size = case_when(accommodates <= 2 ~ "small", accommodates <= 5 ~ "medium", TRUE ~ "large")` — a 3-guest flat is "medium" because the first condition already failed |
| `str_detect(x, pattern)` | TRUE when the pattern appears anywhere in the string (from 2.3) |
| `str_count(x, pattern)` | how many times the pattern appears in the string |
| `str_extract(x, pattern)` | pull out the first fragment of text matching the pattern |
| `year(date)` | the year of a date — same family as `month()`, `day()`, `wday()` |
| `regex("...", ignore_case = TRUE)` | wrap a pattern to make it case-insensitive |

**Sprint 2** ⏱ 15:00 — your turn to clean. Extend `listings` with:

1. `n_amenities`: how many amenities each listing advertises (count the commas in `amenities` with `str_count()` and add 1). What's the median? And the maximum — is it plausible?
2. `price_person`: price per accommodated guest
3. `long_stay`: TRUE when `minimum_nights` ≥ 30 (these are not tourist rentals — how many are there?)
4. `listed_year`: the year the listing entered the market (proxy: `year(first_review)` — check what `host_since` contains in this snapshot before reaching for it!)
5. `license_status`: `"licensed"` when `license` contains a `"VT-"` tourist-licence number, `"exempt"` when it mentions Exempt, `"none"` when missing, `"other"` otherwise (`case_when` + `str_detect` — mind the order of the branches!). What share is licensed?
6. *Stretch:* some hosts SHOUT. How many `name`s contain **no lowercase letters at all**? (`str_detect` with pattern `"^[^a-z]+$"` — a character class: from start `^` to end `$`, only characters that are *not* a–z.)

```{r ex02}
listings <- listings |>
  mutate(
    n_amenities = str_count(amenities, ",") + 1,
    price_person = price_eur / accommodates,
    long_stay = minimum_nights >= 30,
    listed_year = year(first_review),
    license_status = case_when(
      is.na(license) ~ "none",
      str_detect(license, "VT-") ~ "licensed",
      str_detect(license, regex("exempt", ignore_case = T)) ~ "licensed",
      TRUE ~ "other"
    )
  )

listings |> summarise(median_amen = median(n_amenities), max_amen = max(n_amenities))
glimpse(listings)
```

# Block 3 · Transform, tidy & join ⏱ 60′

## 3.1 · The dplyr verbs, all together now

Each takes a table, returns a table — that's why they chain:

```{r}
listings |>
  filter(room_type == "Entire home/apt", is_active,          # rows
         neighbourhood_cleansed == "RUSSAFA") |>   # barrios are UPPERCASE in the data!
  select(name, accommodates, price_eur, review_scores_rating) |>   # columns
  arrange(desc(review_scores_rating)) |>                     # order
  head(5)
```

Top to bottom:

* `filter(...)` — keep rows: entire homes, active, in Russafa (comma-separated conditions combine with AND; note the data spells barrios in UPPERCASE — `== "Russafa"` would silently match *nothing*);
* `select(...)` — keep four columns;
* `arrange(desc(...))` — sort by rating, best first;
* `head(5)` — show five.

Each verb takes a table and returns a table — the chain never breaks, and the code is its own documentation.

`select()` also takes helpers — `starts_with("review_scores")`, `contains("host")`, `where(is.numeric)` — and with 90 columns you will want them.

## 3.2 · Grouped summaries — the heart of EDA

Half of all EDA questions have the same shape: *compute X **per** group*. The answer is always the same two-step — **`group_by()` splits, `summarise()` collapses**:

* `group_by(barrio = neighbourhood_cleansed)` — split into one mini-table per barrio (renaming the column on the fly);
* `summarise(...)` — reduce each mini-table to a single row, computing whatever you ask:
  * `n()` — how many rows landed in this group (no arguments needed);
  * `median(price_eur)` — a robust centre;
  * `mean(logical)` — our proportion trick ("share of superhosts");
* the result is itself a small table — one row per barrio — to filter and rank like any other:

```{r}
barrio_stats <- listings |>
  filter(!is.na(price_eur)) |>
  group_by(barrio = neighbourhood_cleansed) |>
  summarise(n            = n(),
            median_price = median(price_eur),
            share_super  = mean(host_is_superhost, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  filter(n >= 20)                       # don't rank on 3 listings!

barrio_stats |> slice_max(median_price, n = 5)
barrio_stats |> slice_min(median_price, n = 5)
```

`slice_max()` / `slice_min()` show the two ends of the ranking. Read the tables like an analyst, not a printer:

* **top** — the historic centre (El Mercat, la Seu, Sant Francesc) plus Penya-roja and the Cabanyal beachfront;
* **bottom** — peripheral, residential barrios;
* every row carries its `n`: you always know how much data stands behind each median — exactly why the `filter(n >= 20)` guard exists.

> 💡 Try the ranking *without* the `filter(n >= 20)` line: a barrio with 3 listings takes the top spot, and adding the guard changes the podium. Never rank groups without checking group size.

## 3.3 · Reshaping with tidyr: `pivot_wider` / `pivot_longer`

A question like *"median price per district **and** room type"* produces **long** data: one row per district × room-type combination — perfect for computing, awkward for humans, who want a grid (districts as rows, room types as columns):

* `pivot_wider(names_from = , values_from = )` — one new **column** per value of `names_from`, filled with the numbers in `values_from`;
* `pivot_longer()` — the inverse: melt columns back into rows (the direction real-world spreadsheets usually need);
* `.groups = "drop"` inside `summarise()` — book-keeping: un-group the result, silence dplyr's message.

```{r}
price_table <- listings |>
  filter(!is.na(price_eur)) |>
  group_by(district = neighbourhood_group_cleansed, room_type) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price_eur), .groups = "drop")

price_table |> head(4)                                  # long: one row per combo

price_wide <- price_table |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = room_type, values_from = median_price)
price_wide |> head(6)                                   # wide: one row per district

# and back - pivot_longer is how you *tidy* spreadsheet-shaped data:
price_wide |> pivot_longer(-district,
                           names_to = "room_type", values_to = "median_price") |> head(4)
```

## 3.4 · One value per cell: `separate_rows()` on `amenities` *(stretch)*

`amenities` crams a whole list into one cell — `["Wifi", "Kitchen", ...]` — breaking tidy data's *one value per cell* rule. Two moves untangle it:

* `str_remove_all()` — delete every bracket and quote (the pattern `'[\\[\\]"]'` is a character class listing the three symbols to delete);
* `separate_rows(amenities, sep = ", ")` — split each cell at the commas: **each amenity gets its own row**;
* the table explodes from ~8,000 rows to a few hundred thousand — precisely what makes amenities countable with `count()`:

```{r}
amen <- listings |>
  select(id, amenities) |>
  mutate(amenities = str_remove_all(amenities, '[\\[\\]"]')) |>
  separate_rows(amenities, sep = ", ")

amen |> count(amenities, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)
# share of listings with air conditioning - in València, not a detail:
amen |> filter(amenities == "Air conditioning") |> nrow() / nrow(listings)
```

## 3.5 · More than one table: joins

Real analyses are multi-table. Ours also has `reviews.csv.gz` — one row per review. A **join** matches rows of two tables through a shared key column. The one you will use 90% of the time:

* `left_join(A, B)` — **enrich**: every row of A survives, gaining B's columns where the key matches; rows with no match get NA.

The rest of the family, for when you need them: `inner_join()` keeps only the rows that match in *both* tables; `right_join()` and `full_join()` change which side survives (all of B / all of both); `anti_join()` returns the rows of A *without* a match in B — useful for spotting misspelled or outdated keys. Same syntax as `left_join()` in every case.

Two helpers before the first join:

* `tribble()` — write a small tibble row by row: perfect for hand-made lookup tables like the one below;
* `join_by(a == b)` — declare which column of the left table matches which of the right;
* unmatched left-table rows survive with NA — we make that explicit with `replace_na()`:

```{r}
# ENRICH with left_join(): attach a zone classification we define ourselves
zones <- tribble(
  ~district,           ~zone,
  "CIUTAT VELLA",      "Centre",
  "L'EIXAMPLE",        "Centre",
  "EXTRAMURS",         "Centre",
  "POBLATS MARITIMS",  "Beach",     # note: the data spells districts WITHOUT
  "CAMINS AL GRAU",    "Beach",     # accents - copy strings exactly as they
  "ALGIROS",           "Beach",     # appear, or the join silently misses
)

listings <- listings |>
  left_join(zones, join_by(neighbourhood_group_cleansed == district)) |>
  mutate(zone = replace_na(zone, "Rest of the city"))   # unmatched rows got NA

listings |> count(zone)
```

```{r}
# The reviews file: one row per review, ~450k rows. Depending on the snapshot
# it has 2 columns (listing_id, date) or 6 (+ review id, reviewer, comments) -
# we only use two of them.
reviews <- read_csv("data/reviews.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(reviews)
class(reviews$date)   # check before trusting: dates wear costumes too

# In some files the date arrives as TEXT like "12/10/2010" (day/month/year).
# Then max(date) would compare it alphabetically - silently wrong.
# Parse it explicitly; if readr already made it a Date, leave it be:
reviews <- reviews |>
  mutate(date = if (is.character(date)) dmy(date) else date)

rev_stats <- reviews |>
  group_by(listing_id) |>
  summarise(n_rev_file = n(), last_rev_file = max(date))

listings <- listings |>
  left_join(rev_stats, join_by(id == listing_id)) |>
  mutate(n_rev_file = replace_na(n_rev_file, 0))        # no match = zero reviews

# audit: does the reviews file agree with number_of_reviews?
listings |> summarise(agreement = mean(n_rev_file == number_of_reviews))
```

> ⚠️ If you peek at `reviews.csv.gz` in **Excel** you may see dates reshuffled to your locale and accents mangled into `Ã©`, `Ã­`... That is Excel guessing wrong, not the data: the file is UTF-8 and R reads it correctly. Inspect data with R, not with a spreadsheet.

> 💡 **The join ritual.** `left_join` + `replace_na` + a check, every time you join:
>
> * *keep everything* — `left_join` never drops rows from the left table;
> * *make absence explicit* — `replace_na` turns "no match" into a real value (here: 0 reviews);
> * *verify* — compare against a second source (`number_of_reviews` from the listings file). Agreement is high but rarely 1.0: deleted reviews, files scraped on different days, listings removed between scrapes.

🧰 **Sprint toolbox**:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `slice_max(col, n = 10)` | the 10 rows with the largest `col` (`slice_min()` = smallest); after `group_by()` it works *per group* — add `with_ties = FALSE` to force exactly one row each |
| `pull(col)` | extract one column as a plain vector — the pipe-friendly `$` |
| `mean(logical_col)` | share of TRUEs: the idiom for proportions ("share of superhosts") |
| `x %in% set` | membership test from HW0 — handy for filtering by a list of ids |

# Block 4 · Wrap-up

One save, so that today's work travels to Session 2 — `write_rds()` keeps every column type intact:

```{r save}
write_rds(listings, "data/listings_clean.rds")
dim(listings)
```

**Today in one slide:**

* **Import** — `read_csv()` (gz included); meet the data with `glimpse()`, `skim()`, `count()`, `n_distinct()`; `clean_names()` as a reflex.
* **Clean** — `parse_number()` for money; `str_detect/replace/extract/count` for text; `interval()` + `time_length()` for dates; `case_when()` for categories; NAs: audit before dropping — missingness can be *structural* (our price ↔ availability).
* **Transform** — the verbs `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`; the two-step `group_by() |> summarise()`; rank with `slice_max/min`, never without `n`.
* **Tidy & join** — `pivot_wider/longer`, `separate_rows`; `left_join` to enrich (`inner`, `right`, `full`, `anti` for the other flavours), `replace_na` afterwards.
* **Habits** — check the type before trusting (`glimpse`, `class`); strings must match *exactly* (UPPERCASE barrios!); if it doesn't knit, it doesn't exist.

That clean table is where Session 2 starts: we *look* at it (ggplot2), interrogate it (EDA), and model it.

**Before Session 2 HW1, on Poliformat:**

* three extra notebooks (dplyr, stringr, lubridate) — further practice.
* one **optional chore**: aggregate `calendar.csv.gz` (~3 million rows!) into a monthly availability/price table per listing.
